Nikhil Gupta stands as he is sentenced by U.S. District Judge Victor Marrero in federal court in New York City on November 20, 2026, in this courtroom sketch. | Photo Credit: Reuters

Indian national Nikhil Gupta was sentenced to 235 months in jail by a U.S. court on Friday (November 20, 2026) for his involvement in a murder-for-hire plot against a Sikh extremist on American soil.

Gupta, 55, had pleaded guilty earlier this year to charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering, in connection with his efforts to murder Khalistani separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York.

Judge Victor Marrero of the Southern District of New York announced 235 months prison term to Gupta after an almost 80-minute hearing.

The judge did not impose any sentence of supervised release on Gupta, saying he will be put in deportation and removal proceedings once he completes the prison term.

Also Read | Pannun’s civil lawsuit: U.S. court allows Pannun to serve NSA Doval and former intelligence chief Goyal

Gupta, wearing a tan prison suit, was escorted into the courtroom by marshals. He scanned the room as he entered and sat flanked by his lawyers.

Gupta invoked the teachings of Mahatma Gandhi, Mother Teresa, Nelson Mandela and Martin Luther King and said he had hoped to live by the ideals of these leaders.

Gupta apologised for his actions in a brief six-minute statement that he delivered in English in court.

“I cannot undo what I have done. I am sorry to Pannun, to the community and the fraternity. I’m sorry,” Gupta said, turning to look at Pannun, who was seated in the courtroom and had several members of the Sikh community accompanying him for the hearing.

stories.title: Indian man sentenced to 19 years in prison for conspiring to kill Sikh separatist in New York
stories.dek: Nikhil Gupta admitted to plotting with Indian government official to hire hitman to murder dual US-Canadian citizen An Indian ⁠man was sentenced to more ⁠than 19 ​years in US prison on Friday after ad…
stories.content:
A courtroom sketch of Nikhil Gupta in court in New York City on 17 June 2024. Photograph: Jane Rosenberg/Reuters View image in fullscreen A courtroom sketch of Nikhil Gupta in court in New York City on 17 June 2024. Photograph: Jane Rosenberg/Reuters New York Indian man sentenced to 19 years in prison for conspiring to kill Sikh separatist in New York Nikhil Gupta admitted to plotting with Indian government official to hire hitman to murder dual US-Canadian citizen

An Indian ⁠man was sentenced to more ⁠than 19 ​years in US prison on Friday after admitting to orchestrating a failed Indian government-backed plot to kill a Sikh separatist in New York ⁠City , in connection with what US and Canadian authorities have called a broader effort to target Indian dissidents.

Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy ⁠to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

The US district judge Victor Marrero handed down the ​235-month sentence at a hearing in a Manhattan federal ‌court.

The discovery of alleged ‌assassination plots against Sikh separatists in the US and Canada has tested relations with India , which has ‌denied involvement in such plots.

Prosecutors accused Gupta of plotting with an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer at Sikhs for Justice in New York who has advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.

Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in cash delivered to a purported hitman who ‌was actually an undercover US law enforcement officer, court papers show.

Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear ​whether he has hired a defense lawyer.

India’s government has dissociated itself from any plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.

Prosecutors with the Manhattan US attorney’s office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison.

“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley ⁠Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices ​in this country, ever.”

Addressing the ​court on Friday, Gupta said ​he regretted straying from the non-violent example set by the Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi .

“I’m ​sorry to Mr ‌Pannun, I’m sorry ​to the communities I hurt, ​I’m sorry to my own family,” Gupta said.

stories.title: Iran has been ‘bullsh–ting people for 51 years,’ wants ‘fake deal’ to end war, Trump says
stories.dek: "They want to make a deal, but they don't want to make a deal that's acceptable to me," Trump said during a lengthy lunchtime news conference Friday at the White House
stories.content:
President Trump accused Iran Friday of trying to get a “fake deal” to end the almost nine-month-old war — saying the Islamic Republic has been “bulls—ting people” for years.

Follow The Post’s live coverage of President Trump and national politics for the latest news and analysis

“They want to make a deal, but they don’t want to make a deal that’s acceptable to me,” the president said during a lengthy lunchtime news conference at the White House, one day after returning from a whirlwind three-day trip to Asia.

“We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal that they’ve been doing for 51 years,” Trump said. “They’ve been bulls—ting people for 51 years.”

Trump mentioned Iran after celebrating a recent drop in oil prices , saying that future costs “also depend on how we settle up with Iran.”

“I’m not George Bush — ‘watch my lips’ — no, you don’t have to watch my lips. But Iran will never have a nuclear weapon ever,” he said.

Both Trump and Vice President JD Vance have said the landslide Republican defeat in this month’s midterm elections was caused by the war, which caused higher energy prices and inflation.

Vance joined Trump at the press conference and was asked about his post-election suggestion that the conflict wasn’t worth it.

“The president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again,” Vance said. “My goal is, and my job is, to support the president of the United States.”

The president did not say what progress he may have notched toward ending the war during meetings in Shenzhen, China, where he spoke privately with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump also acknowledged recent reporting that Iran may be considering attacking the nation’s capital with a so-called “dirty bomb.” “There is a rumor that they’re building a dirty bomb ,” Trump said. “If they are, we’ll find out about it. We will not allow that.”

The president said last week that the war he launched in February was “effectively over” but that he plans to leave in place an economically ruinous blockade of Iranian ports unless Tehran agrees to give up its nuclear program.

stories.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
stories.dek: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn't stay private.
stories.content:
Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private.

Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

stories.title: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
stories.dek: Scientists have discovered a faster way to identify diamond-based materials that could power quantum computers and sensors at room temperature.
stories.content:
A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

stories.title: Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Agreements and Regional Energy Corridors
stories.dek: A multi-perspective assessment of offshore natural gas transit frameworks, maritime boundary negotiations, and regional stability.
stories.content:
The Eastern Mediterranean basin continues to navigate complex multilateral diplomatic engagements balancing offshore energy exploration with sovereign boundary delimitation. High-level delegations from regional coastal states and European partners are refining frameworks that align pipeline routes with equitable maritime economic zones.

Key Perspectives & Strategic Dimensions:
1. Energy Transit Security: Multilateral agreements between Mediterranean states prioritize uninterrupted transit of natural gas to Southern European ports, diversifying continental supply lines.
2. Maritime Boundary Delimitation: Diplomatic mediators emphasize that long-term maritime stability necessitates transparent dispute-resolution mechanisms that account for sovereign continental shelf claims.
3. Regional Economic Interdependence: Joint infrastructure investments in subsea interconnectors create economic mutual interest, offering pragmatic stabilization incentives across diverse stakeholders.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly impacts the economic stability, energy infrastructure, and security landscape across the Levant and Mediterranean.

stories.title: Sub-Microsecond Spin Dynamics in Diamond NV Centers: Benchmarking Cavity QED and Coherence Limits
stories.dek: Mitigating dipolar spin-spin dephasing and hyperfine bath interactions in dense diamond NV ensembles via Floquet driving.
stories.content:
Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) color centers in diamond remain the preeminent solid-state platform for room-temperature quantum metrology and nanoscale magnetic resonance. Scaling from isolated defects to dense ensembles requires overcoming collective dephasing from the surrounding 13C nuclear spin bath.

Recent breakthroughs utilizing microwave cavity coupling and Floquet dynamical decoupling extend the effective coherence time (T2*) by an order of magnitude.

Key Technical Highlights:
1. Cooperative Purcell Enhancement: Dense NV ensembles entering the collective strong coupling regime demonstrate cavity-mediated coherence preservation.
2. Suppression of Spin-Diffusion Loss: Operating within crystallographic symmetry subspaces eliminates cross-axis relaxation.
3. Room-Temperature Sensing: Sustained microsecond coherence enables sub-picotesla magnetic field sensitivities for single-cell NMR.
stories.whyItMatters: Informs room-temperature diamond quantum magnetometry, microwave cavity loading, and advanced Floquet decoupling protocols in spin dynamics.

stories.source: Innatera & Edge AI Insights • 5 min read
stories.title: Sub-Milliwatt Neuromorphic Microcontrollers Shift Real-Time AI Inference to the Edge
stories.dek: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) on silicon processors achieve microsecond response times at sub-milliwatt power budgets.
stories.content:
The paradigm of routing sensor telemetry to centralized cloud servers is rapidly transitioning to on-device neuromorphic microcontrollers. Utilizing event-driven spiking neural architectures, silicon accelerators process acoustic and vibration patterns with near-zero latency.

Key Highlights:
1. In-Memory Processing: Spiking architectures circumvent the classical von Neumann memory bottleneck, consuming less than 1 mW.
2. Zero Cloud Exposure: Sensitive sensor streams remain strictly local, guaranteeing privacy and continuous operation during network blackouts.
3. Predictive Maintenance: Deployed microcontrollers classify industrial vibrations and structural stress in real time.
stories.whyItMatters: Enables zero-latency, private, on-device anomaly detection and vibration monitoring without cloud roundtrips.

stories.title: Circadian Photonic Priming and Equanimity in Demanding Research
stories.dek: Aligning 90-minute ultradian deep work blocks with natural circadian rhythms and secular Buddhist non-reactivity.
stories.content:
Sustained high-level analytical performance requires deliberate biological pacing. Structuring the day around 90-minute ultradian cycles followed by brief decompression intervals prevents cognitive fatigue.

Core Evidence-Based Habits:
1. Photonic Lock: Direct outdoor light exposure within 45 minutes of waking aligns the suprachiasmatic nucleus master clock.
2. Ultradian Block: Dedicate the primary 9:00 AM - 10:30 AM window to pure theoretical derivation before checking correspondence.
3. Secular Equanimity (Dhammapada 81): 'Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.'
stories.whyItMatters: Protects cognitive bandwidth and prevents attentional fragmentation during demanding laboratory derivations.

papers.title: Thermally Activated Magnetic Switching in Antiferromagnetic Van der Waals Trilayers Resolved by Single-Spin Diamond Magnetometry
papers.authors: Fabian A. Gerritsma, Roland W. Mulder, Balázs Nagyfalusi et al.
papers.tldr: Van der Waals magnets provide a versatile platform for exploring magnetic phenomena that emerge from reduced dimensionality, including layer-dependent magnetic ordering. Here, we use scanning nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond magnetometry to measure the magnetization of a trilayer of the A-type antiferromagnet CrPS$_4$, resolving its zero-field bistability between the up-down-up ($\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow$) and down-up-down ($\downarrow\uparrow\downarrow$) layer magnetization configurations.
takeaways: Van der Waals magnets provide a versatile platform for exploring magnetic phenomena that emerge from reduced dimensionality, including layer-dependent magnetic ordering.

Here, we use scanning nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond magnetometry to measure the magnetization of a trilayer of the A-type antiferromagnet CrPS$_4$, resolving its zero-field bistability between the up-down-up ($\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow$) and down-up-down ($\downarrow\uparrow\downarrow$) layer magnetization configurations.

Our results highlight the power of scanning NV magnetometry for the quantitative investigation of magnetization reversal in two-dimensional magnets, unraveling the magnetic phenomenology that emerges in low-dimensional systems.

papers.title: Bright and Uniform Silicon Carbide Nanophotonic Arrays for Scalable Nanoscale Quantum Sensing
papers.authors: Chenyang Liao, Chihang Luo, Xin Chen et al.
papers.tldr: Silicon carbide (SiC) spin defects are emerging as powerful platforms for nanoscale quantum sensing due to their near-surface stability, near-infrared emission, and CMOS compatibility. However, poor photon collection efficiency and the reliance on randomly distributed defects hinder the realization of practical, large-scale devices.
takeaways: Silicon carbide (SiC) spin defects are emerging as powerful platforms for nanoscale quantum sensing due to their near-surface stability, near-infrared emission, and CMOS compatibility.
Furthermore, we apply these devices to nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), successfully demonstrating external nanoscale nuclear-spin detection.
These results establish our SiC nanopillars as robust building blocks for scanning quantum probes and scalable sensor networks.

papers.title: Algorithmic Quantum Sensing
papers.authors: Ishaan Kannan, Aditi Venkatesh, Jordan Cotler
papers.tldr: We introduce a unified framework for sensing time-dependent fields through the lens of classical and quantum algorithms. First, we develop three pulse sequence protocols, namely randomized, matched, and pooled spectroscopy, which outperform established approaches such as dynamical decoupling across a wide range of tasks.
takeaways: First, we develop three pulse sequence protocols, namely randomized, matched, and pooled spectroscopy, which outperform established approaches such as dynamical decoupling across a wide range of tasks.
These protocols attain the optimal sensitivity for linear and nonlinear AC sensing on conventional spin or qubit platforms, improving existing devices by changing only their pulse sequences.

Our result provides the first asymptotic, beyond-quadratic quantum advantage in AC metrology when noise is aligned with the signal, proving that Lindblad span conditions do not apply to broadband quantum sensing.

papers.title: To predict or to persist: how decoherence shapes learning in a spin-qubit quantum reservoir
papers.tldr: In this work we investigate how dephasing and the choice of measured observables affect learning in a simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation and exact expectation-value readout. For externally driven nonlinear autoregressive moving-average signals, combining single- and two-qubit observables gives better predictions than a population-only readout at comparable polynomial feature counts.
takeaways: In this work we investigate how dephasing and the choice of measured observables affect learning in a simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation and exact expectation-value readout.
We do not find a clear systematic dependence of limit-cycle persistence on coherence across the reservoir ensemble.
We conclude that, within this simulated reservoir, the impact of coherence depends strongly on the task.

papers.title: Spin dynamics in disordered systems with generic spin-momentum couplings: A matrix-rational formulation
papers.tldr: We develop a microscopic framework for the disorder-averaged density-matrix dynamics of pseudospin-$1/2$ systems with anisotropic and nonlinear spin-momentum couplings. Starting from the Diffuson, we introduce a matrix-valued rational approximation for its frequency dependence that does not rely on a low-frequency or weak-coupling expansion.
takeaways: We develop a microscopic framework for the disorder-averaged density-matrix dynamics of pseudospin-$1/2$ systems with anisotropic and nonlinear spin-momentum couplings.

Comparisons with direct numerical simulations demonstrate quantitative agreement for both the post-quench spin dynamics and spin relaxation times across a broad range of coupling strengths, extending beyond the diffusive regime.
The matrix-rational formulation provides a unified description of ultrafast spin dynamics and long-time relaxation.
